walkthroughs.body_html:
For a spring: F = k × e.

F is the force in newtons, k is the spring constant in N/m, and e is the extension in metres.

Double the force, double the extension — but only up to the limit of proportionality. Past that, the spring stops obeying Hooke. 🪀

A stretched spring stores energy. E = ½ × k × e².

If k = 200 N/m and you stretch it by 0.1 m, stored energy is ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J.

Release the spring and that energy becomes kinetic — boing!

A skydiver speeds up because weight > air resistance. As they speed up, air resistance grows.

Eventually air resistance equals weight. Resultant force = 0. The skydiver stops accelerating and falls at a steady terminal velocity.

Open the parachute — air resistance jumps up, they slow down, then reach a new (slower) terminal velocity. 🪂

mcqs.q: At terminal velocity, the resultant force on a falling object is:
options: Equal to weight
Zero
Greater than air resistance
Negative

mcqs.q: Which is the correct formula for elastic potential energy?
options: E = k × e
E = ½ × k × e
E = ½ × k × e²
E = m × g × h

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Mass changes with location but weight does not.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N) and depends on g.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.
Mass and weight are the same thing, just expressed in different units.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
